title: Ratios & Proportions
coreInsight: A ratio describes a multiplicative relationship or repeatable batch, and proportional situations preserve that relationship as quantities scale.
targetLearnerRealization: A ratio is a repeatable multiplicative batch; scaling one quantity requires scaling the corresponding quantity by the same factor.
learningObjectives: Interpret a ratio as a repeatable batch.
Scale corresponding quantities by the same factor.
Recognize and complete proportional relationships without relying on cross-multiplication as a starting rule.

continuity.openingCallback: Return to the red and blue counters and distinguish a direct comparison from a part-whole fraction.
closingSeeds: A ratio can compare quantities carrying different units.
Dividing both quantities by the same count can reveal an amount per one unit.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Ratio problems should be solved by additive differences.
Part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios are interchangeable.
Cross-multiplication is the meaning of proportion rather than one consequence of it.
Corresponding quantities can be paired in any order.

beats.purpose: Use the predecessor's counter mixture to distinguish part-to-part and part-to-whole comparisons.
beats.expectedRealization: The same objects support different ratios depending on what is being compared.
beats.transitionIn: The bag held 3 red counters and 5 blue counters. Keep the objects, but change the comparison.
beats.prompt: Which pair correctly describes red-to-blue and red-to-total, in that order?

visual.ariaLabel: Three red counters and five blue counters

beats.correctFeedback: Right. Red-to-blue compares 3 with 5; red-to-total compares 3 with all 8.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Name the two quantities in order before writing their counts.

steps.title: Read the order
steps.body: Red-to-blue is 3:5 because those groups contain 3 and 5 counters.

steps.title: Change the second quantity
steps.body: Red-to-total is 3:8 because the whole bag contains 3 + 5 = 8 counters.

resolution.takeaway: A ratio's order and named quantities are part of its meaning.

beats.purpose: Discover proportional scaling by duplicating an authentic 4-to-7 batch.
beats.expectedRealization: Reaching 28 sports cars requires seven whole batches, so the paired sedan count must also scale sevenfold.
beats.transitionIn: The 3-to-5 counter relationship was one batch. Now watch a 4-to-7 relationship repeat until its first count reaches a target.
beats.whyNow: The authentic sports-car/sedan relationship literally displays the lesson's core multiplicative structure as repeatable batches.
beats.entryBridge: Treat 4 sports cars paired with 7 sedans as one indivisible batch.
beats.exitBridge: Seven copies of both sides preserve the relationship: 4:7 becomes 28:49.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Two named groups held together as one batch, extending the red-and-blue counter comparison.
learnerPrompts: At the first step, identify the two counts in one batch.
When the empty batch slots appear, compute 28 ÷ 4 to decide how many copies are needed.
At the warning step, explain why multiplying 28 by 4 scales the wrong quantity.
When sedans appear in every batch, count 7 groups of 7.
Use the final check to verify both quantities were multiplied by 7.
beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Seven complete 4-to-7 batches contain 28 sports cars and 49 sedans.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Find how many groups of 4 make 28, then use that same number of groups of 7.

steps.title: Count batches
steps.body: 28 ÷ 4 = 7, so the target contains seven copies of the original batch.

steps.title: Scale the partner
steps.body: Each batch contains 7 sedans, so seven batches contain 7 × 7 = 49 sedans.

steps.title: Check both sides
steps.body: 4 × 7 = 28 and 7 × 7 = 49. Both corresponding quantities used the same scale factor, so the answer is D.

resolution.takeaway: Scale both quantities by the same factor.

beats.purpose: Contrast multiplicative scaling with preserving an additive difference.
beats.expectedRealization: A constant difference does not preserve a ratio.
beats.transitionIn: The original batch had three more sedans than sports cars. Test whether keeping that difference keeps the relationship.
beats.prompt: Starting from 4 sports cars to 7 sedans, which pair preserves the same relationship?

options.text: 8 sports cars to 11 sedans, because both increased by 4.
8 sports cars to 14 sedans, because both counts doubled.
12 sports cars to 15 sedans, because the difference stays 3.
7 sports cars to 4 sedans, because the counts are unchanged.

beats.incorrectFeedback: Ask whether each new count is the same multiple of its original count.

steps.title: Reject additive thinking
steps.body: The pair 8:11 keeps the difference 3, but 8/11 is not equal to 4/7.

resolution.takeaway: Proportions preserve multiplication, not a fixed difference.

beats.purpose: Show that shrinking or enlarging whole batches produces equivalent ratios.
beats.expectedRealization: Dividing both counts by a common factor reveals the same simplest batch.
beats.transitionIn: A batch can be repeated. It can also be grouped back into smaller identical batches.
beats.prompt: Which ratio describes the same red-to-blue relationship as 6:10?
beats.correctFeedback: Right. Dividing both counts by 2 reveals the 3-to-5 batch.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use one common divisor on both quantities and preserve their order.

visual.ariaLabel: Six red units and ten blue units grouped as two copies of a three-to-five batch

steps.body: 6:10 = (2 × 3):(2 × 5). Removing the common factor 2 leaves 3:5 without changing the relationship.

resolution.takeaway: Equivalent ratios are scaled copies of one batch.

beats.purpose: Make correspondence and order explicit before proportion notation is formalized.
beats.expectedRealization: Each position must continue to name the same quantity across equivalent ratios.
beats.transitionIn: Scaling preserves a batch only if the same kinds of quantities stay aligned.
beats.prompt: A paint mix uses 3 cups blue for every 5 cups white. Which equality keeps corresponding colors in the same positions?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Blue stays over blue, white stays over white, and both counts are tripled.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Label the numerator and denominator on both sides before checking the scale factor.

steps.body: 3 blue becomes 9 blue and 5 white becomes 15 white. Thus 3/5 = 9/15. Reversing only one side changes which quantities correspond.

resolution.takeaway: Keep labels and order attached to ratio numbers.

beats.purpose: Name ratios and proportions after repeated batches, scale factors, and correspondence have been experienced.
beats.expectedRealization: A proportion states that two ordered comparisons preserve one multiplicative relationship.
beats.transitionIn: The car batches and paint batches used the same structure.
beats.name: Ratio and proportion
beats.conciseDefinition: A ratio compares two quantities in a stated order. A proportion says that two ratios describe the same multiplicative relationship.
beats.formalization: a:b = ka:kb, or a/b = ka/kb, for a nonzero scale factor k
beats.memoryHook: Same labels, same order, same scale factor.

beats.purpose: Require independent proportional scaling in a new context.
beats.expectedRealization: The scale factor can be found from either corresponding pair and applied to the other.
beats.transitionIn: Use the named structure without car icons or a written cross-product rule.
beats.prompt: A model uses 5 square pieces for every 2 triangular pieces. A larger model has 8 triangular pieces. How many square pieces preserve the design?

response.feedback: Compare 8 triangles with the original 2 triangles, then scale the 5 squares by the same factor.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The triangle count is multiplied by 4, so the square count is also multiplied by 4.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Eight triangles make four batches of two triangles. Each batch needs five squares.

steps.title: Find the scale
steps.body: 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so the larger model contains four original batches.

steps.title: Check correspondence
steps.body: 5:2 and 20:8 both compare squares with triangles and both simplify to the same batch.

resolution.takeaway: Find the batch count from one pair; apply it to the corresponding partner.

beats.purpose: Consolidate ratio meaning before introducing rates.
beats.expectedRealization: Order, labels, and common scaling jointly determine a proportion.
beats.transitionIn: The contexts changed, but every valid comparison passed the same checks.
beats.prompt: Select every condition required for two ratios to describe the same proportional relationship.

options.text: Corresponding positions name the same kinds of quantities.
Both quantities are scaled by the same factor.
The difference between the two counts stays fixed.
One ratio may be reversed without changing the other.

response.feedback: Think about what made 4:7 equal 28:49 and what made 3/5 equal 9/15.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Labels and order identify the comparison; a shared factor preserves it.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A fixed difference and a one-sided reversal do not preserve a multiplicative batch.

steps.title: Name
steps.body: State which quantities occupy the first and second positions.

steps.title: Scale
steps.body: Multiply or divide both corresponding counts by the same nonzero factor.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Reduce both ratios to the same batch or compare their matching scale factors.

resolution.takeaway: A proportion preserves an ordered, labeled multiplicative relationship.

beats.purpose: Create the forward need for rates by attaching unlike units and asking for a per-one comparison.
beats.expectedRealization: A ratio with different units can be scaled to describe an amount per one unit.
beats.transitionIn: So far the paired counts were cars with cars or colors with colors. Now let the two sides carry different units.
beats.prompt: A cyclist travels 36 miles in 3 hours. Which question would turn this ratio into a useful per-one comparison?

options.text: How many miles are traveled in 1 hour?
How many hours are in 36 miles without choosing an order?

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Scaling 36 miles in 3 hours down to one hour creates miles per hour.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep the ordered quantities and ask what amount corresponds to exactly one hour.

steps.body: Divide both quantities by 3: 36 miles in 3 hours becomes 12 miles in 1 hour. The relationship now carries a compound unit—miles per hour—which will guide both meaning and calculation.

resolution.takeaway: A per-one ratio with units is a rate.

notes: The approved 2009 bank problem is the discovery anchor; later micro-checks contrast multiplicative and additive reasoning.
The lesson remains draft pending human pedagogical review.
